On that island nation, small earthquakes are frequent, and Icelanders have learned to live with tremors that cause the ground to rumble and shake. But this event was beyond what Icelanders were used to. Thousands of earthquakes, big and small, were felt all around the island for weeks. The earthquakes were a signal of a historic event in the making. On March 19, 2021, it happened. The earth at
(pronounced FAH-grah-dal-sfyalt) broke open, and molten lava began to pour out.

textContent.text: Iceland, which is situated between the Greenland Sea and the North Atlantic Ocean, is one of the most volcanic places in the world. Iceland's volcanoes are world-famous, especially Mount Hekla, the island's most active volcano. In fact, a major volcanic event occurs in Iceland about every five years! But on the Reykjanes Peninsula, the home of Mount Fagradalsfjall, there hadn't been any volcanic activity in about eight hundred years. That was until lava began gushing up from nine miles below the earth's surface and spewing out of a vent. It flowed across the barren, rocky land.

During the eruption, the landscape began to change. Unlike some eruptions that are sudden and quick, this one lasted for an unusually long time. New vents formed, and lava from these vents flowed far and wide, creeping across the land. Six months after the eruption began, fresh lava continued to spread. It filled the valley closest to the eruption site and kept going, over ridges and into other valleys. The earth rumbled, making it sound as if there were thunder below the surface.

The eruption was thrilling to behold. Often volcanic activity can only be observed from far away, but the Fagradalsfjall eruption was different. Because of the lava's slow flow, people could get shockingly close to it—and many did. Hundreds of thousands of visitors from around the world made the trek to see the volcano. They took selfies close enough to the red hot lava to feel its strong heat. Some even roasted hot dogs and marshmallows over the molten rock. At night, they came to watch lava glow against the dark night sky. While the sight was exciting, it was also dangerous to be that close. Volcanic activity is unpredictable. Authorities warned people about the dangers, and at times there were evacuations.

Tourists were not the only people rushing to Mount Fagradalsfjall. For scientists, the volcanic activity was a dream come true. Many scientists observed the volcano on live feeds that were being streamed to labs around the world. Some scientists got on planes to see the volcano for themselves. Then there were the scientists who were lucky enough to already be working in Iceland. They collected samples, compiled data, and used tools like satellites and drones to monitor the volcano's activity.

Eventually, the eruption at Mount Fagradalsfjall came to an end. The fiery glow gradually faded from view as the molten lava cooled and hardened. But the legacy of this eruption will endure for years to come. Scientists continue to analyze the data collected during the eruption in order to better understand and prepare for volcanic events in the future. And visitors continue to explore the radically altered landscape around Mount Fagradalsfjall, marveling at evidence of the Earth's transformative power.

textContent.text: In May of 1961, President John F. Kennedy set an ambitious goal: by the end of that decade, the United States would send an astronaut to the moon. Soon after President Kennedy's announcement, NASA began buying land east of Orlando, Florida. This beautiful stretch of coastline was home to alligators, manatees, wild boars—and soon it was home to astronauts! NASA's purchase included Merritt Island, where construction of the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) began in 1962.

Ever since it opened, KSC has served as the starting point for some of the most important U.S. missions into space. It is where the Apollo moon mission got started, as well as missions to the Skylab space station. Many important unmanned space flights also began at KSC. For example, both the Hubble Space Telescope and the Mars rovers launched from the space center.

Hundreds of highly restricted buildings are located at KSC. Some of these buildings contain special "clean rooms," where equipment for space missions can be assembled in a nearly dust-free and germ-free environment. Other buildings act as huge warehouses where rockets are stored for upcoming launches. But KSC is not entirely off-limits. In fact, the public is encouraged to visit the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex. At the visitor complex, guests can learn about NASA's historic accomplishments and current missions.

For some lucky individuals, the highlight of a visit to KSC is experiencing a live rocket launch. At designated viewing locations, space experts share details about the launch with excited crowds. The viewing locations are just a few miles from the launch pads. Not only can visitors see and hear the spacecraft as it lifts off, they can feel the rumbling of the engines, too. For many visitors, participating in the shouts and cheers of a space launch is an indelible experience, lasting long after the roar of the rockets has faded away.

In the KSC Rocket Garden you can walk along a special gantry, or bridge. It is the exact gantry that the Apollo astronauts used while boarding their historic 1969 flight to the moon. If that is not exciting enough, you can also see other actual space shuttles, including
. This shuttle went on thirty-three historic missions, including a 2009 mission to service the Hubble Space Telescope.

You can meet working astronauts and hear about their careers. It is even possible to attend mission status briefings. At these talks, you can learn about ongoing missions and get updates on experiments underway at the International Space Station. With so many different things to see and experience, most people find a visit to KSC to be a total blast!

textContent.text: Imagine you are on a lush, green island surrounded by a sparkling blue sea. It seems like paradise—that is, until you peer into the trees. Creatures with long, golden bodies and beady black eyes are watching you. Look even closer, and you'll see that the island is covered with thousands of golden lancehead snakes. They're crawling on tree branches, hiding under yellow and brown leaves, and sunning themselves on rocks. The island is Ilha da Queimada Grande, Brazil, and it likely has more venomous snakes per acre than anywhere else on the planet. In fact, Ilha da Queimada Grande is commonly called Snake Island.

Lanceheads belong to a family of venomous snakes called pit vipers. A lancehead's venom is so deadly that it can kill a person in less than an hour! So, while the Brazilian government allows boats to go near the island, landing there is prohibited. Usually only a handful of researchers and trained navy sailors are allowed on the island each year. They wear thick boots and watch every step they take. Yet even these experts are not allowed to set foot on the island's rocky coastline unless a doctor carrying special medicine is present. And even that may not save someone who gets bitten.

Among the local fishing folk, there are myths and rumors about the dangers of Ilha da Queimada Grande. One story tells of a man who landed on the island looking for bananas and was never seen alive again. In another story, a family who cared for the island lighthouse in the early 1900s died when snakes broke into their home. Perhaps the wildest tale is about pirates who supposedly buried treasure on the island to be guarded by the snakes.

Whether or not these legends are true, one thing is certain about the island: its famous inhabitants are actually being threatened. It might seem unlikely that this population of deadly snakes would be in danger. After all, they have no natural predators on the island. The snakes of Ilha da Queimada Grande don't have to worry about being eaten by weasels or mongooses as they slither into trees to catch their dinner. Yet human actions are causing some of the snakes to starve. Because of the human destruction of forests on the mainland, fewer birds are flying to the island.

In addition to a dwindling food supply, the golden lancehead also faces the threat of biopiracy. Biopirates are criminals who search for endangered plants and animals, which they then sell illegally to collectors. As a critically endangered animal found only on Ilha da Queimada Grande, a golden lancehead can sell for as much as thirty thousand dollars on the black market. At this price, some biopirates are willing to risk their lives in order to capture one.

Why should we care about the fate of a highly dangerous reptile? One reason is that venomous snakes provide more to humans than most of us realize. These snakes are carefully caught, milked for their venom, and then released. The venom is then used to make life-saving medicines that help with a number of conditions, including heart disease. Experts suspect that snake venom may have even more uses than we currently know about. If the golden lanceheads on Snake Island die out, with them dies the opportunity to learn how their venom may be used in other helpful ways. Although commonly considered a foe, this snake may actually serve as a friend—from a safe distance, of course.

title.text: The Sights and Smells of Varanasi

textContent.text: The streets of Varanasi, India, are a maze of activity. Colorful, time-worn buildings frame the busy narrow streets. Carts of vegetables, mounds of marigold flowers, and stacks of tourist trinkets line the roads. The air is filled with the sound of bells and the smell of sweet chai tea. Cows and monkeys wander past as the people go about their business.

For centuries, Varanasi, one of the oldest cities in the world, has been a cultural center in India. The city is famous for its silk fabrics and fragrant perfumes. It also serves as a place of learning, and its universities are well known. However, what the city is most notable for is its rich religious history. In India, many people practice a religion called Hinduism. For Hindus, Varanasi is a holy city on a sacred river.

Varanasi is located on a bank of the Ganges River, also known as the Ganga. Hindu legend says that the Ganges flowed out of a knot in the hair of a god named Lord Shiva. Whatever its origin, the river has long been a source of life for the many people who live near it. The city's access to this river draws visitors from across India and the world.

People who come to Varanasi for religious purposes are often referred to as pilgrims. More than two million pilgrims visit Varanasi each year, providing important revenue for the city's economy. For many pilgrims, the journey to Varanasi is a once-in-a-lifetime event. They come to pray or perform rituals in one of Varanasi's temples or at one of many spots at the edge of the Ganges.

All along the banks of the Ganges, concrete and stone staircases, called ghats, lead down to the river. There are more than eighty of these staircases in Varanasi, stretching over several miles. From the base of the ghats, pilgrims release floating oil lamps and marigold flowers into the river. Some pilgrims bathe in the river while others drink its water. Boats of all shapes and sizes launch from the ghats and take visitors along the Ganges. On special "burning ghats," the dead are publicly cremated, and their ashes are scattered in the river. Around these ghats, thick smoke often fills the air.

While the Ganges is a symbol of purity, near Varanasi the river is anything but clean. Its pollution endangers the well-being of the millions of people who rely on it. Untreated sewage, or waste water, is the main source of the river's pollution. This sewage makes many people sick each year. For years, India has been committed to a far-reaching program to clean up the river. Removing pollution and rerouting waste water will take time, but there is hope that India's continued efforts will someday result in a clean Ganges for the people of Varanasi and all of its visitors.

textContent.text: The streets of Varanasi, India, are a maze of activity. Colorful, time-worn buildings frame the busy narrow streets. Carts of vegetables, mounds of marigold flowers, and stacks of tourist trinkets line the roads. The air is filled with the sound of bells and the smell of sweet chai tea. Cows and monkeys wander past as the people go about their business.

For centuries, Varanasi, one of the oldest cities in the world, has been a cultural center in India. The city is famous for its silk fabrics and fragrant perfumes. It also serves as a place of learning, and its universities are well known. However, what the city is most notable for is its rich religious history. In India, many people practice a religion called Hinduism. For Hindus, Varanasi is a holy city on a sacred river.

Varanasi is located on a bank of the Ganges River, also known as the Ganga. Hindu legend says that the Ganges flowed out of a knot in the hair of a god named Lord Shiva. Whatever its origin, the river has long been a source of life for the many people who live near it. The city's access to this river draws visitors from across India and the world.

People who come to Varanasi for religious purposes are often referred to as pilgrims. More than two million pilgrims visit Varanasi each year, providing important revenue for the city's economy. For many pilgrims, the journey to Varanasi is a once-in-a-lifetime event. They come to pray or perform rituals in one of Varanasi's temples or at one of many spots at the edge of the Ganges.

All along the banks of the Ganges, concrete and stone staircases, called ghats, lead down to the river. There are more than eighty of these staircases in Varanasi, stretching over several miles. From the base of the ghats, pilgrims release floating oil lamps and marigold flowers into the river. Some pilgrims bathe in the river while others drink its water. Boats of all shapes and sizes launch from the ghats and take visitors along the Ganges. On special "burning ghats," the dead are publicly cremated, and their ashes are scattered in the river. Around these ghats, thick smoke often fills the air.

While the Ganges is a symbol of purity, near Varanasi the river is anything but clean. Its pollution endangers the well-being of the millions of people who rely on it. Untreated sewage, or waste water, is the main source of the river's pollution. This sewage makes many people sick each year. For years, India has been committed to a far-reaching program to clean up the river. Removing pollution and rerouting waste water will take time, but there is hope that India's continued efforts will someday result in a clean Ganges for the people of Varanasi and all of its visitors.

In 1979, Vietnam veterans Jan Scruggs and Robert Doubek started the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund (VVMF). They wanted to create a memorial to honor those who had fought in the war and to provide a space for Americans to grieve and heal. The memorial design was chosen through a contest. The contest rules stated that the designs should not contain political statements and that they should include the names of all Americans who had died in the war or remained missing. The judges were well-known architects, city planners, and other professionals. Designs were submitted "blindly," meaning that the judges didn't know who the designers were. To many people's surprise, the winner of the contest was a twenty-one year old student named Maya Lin. At the time, Lin was still studying architecture and was not yet a professional designer.

At first glance, Lin's design seemed simple: it was a V-shaped wall made of smooth, dark granite, inscribed with the name of every American who had died or gone missing in the war. Lin wanted the memorial to be a symbol of the great loss of life during the war. She also envisioned a place where people could come to remember, reflect, and feel a sense of peace.

The Vietnam Memorial Wall that Maya Lin designed was installed in Constitution Gardens in Washington, D.C. One arm of the wall extends toward the Lincoln Memorial, while the other points toward the Washington Monument. The center of the wall is over ten feet high, while the farthest ends of the arms rise just eight inches above the ground. The entire length of the wall is sunk into the ground, like a gash in the earth. The memorial opened to the public in November 1982. The opening ceremony included a fifty-six-hour reading of the names of the dead.

Initially, there had been opposition from some people who didn't think the design of the wall was appropriate for a military memorial. For this reason, a more traditional sculpture, known as the Three Servicemen Statue, was added to the memorial grounds in 1984. A statue honoring the women who served in the war was also added in 1994. However, the wall remains the centerpiece of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial.

Visiting the wall can be an experience filled with deep emotions. This is true for people who have a personal connection to the Vietnam War and for those who do not. The mood at the wall is often somber. As visitors read the names of those who died, they can see their own faces reflected in the granite. Some people cry. Others pray. Visitors often leave items at the wall, such as flags, photos, flowers, military dog tags, and combat boots. Creating rubbings is another common ritual. Visitors place a piece of paper over a name on the wall and use a pencil or crayon to produce a copy of the name. Many people who lost friends or family members in the war say these rituals help with their healing process. Maya Lin's simple but stunning memorial has proved to be a powerful place to remember, grieve, and heal.

contents.text: The progressive tense describes ongoing actions. It tells about something that is, was, or will be happening. To form the progressive tenses, use a form of the helping verb to be with a main verb ending in -ing.

header.text: The present progressive tense tells about something that is happening right now. It uses a present-tense form of the helping verb to be (is, am, or are).

contents.text: Julie is playing basketball right now.

header.text: The past progressive tense tells about something that was happening in the past. It uses a past-tense form of the helping verb to be (was or were).

contents.text: Seth was talking to Mrs. Jones when the phone rang.

header.text: The future progressive tense tells about something that will be happening in the future. It uses the future-tense form of the helping verb to be (will be).
